history.q: In what year did Morocco regain its independence from France?
history.fact: France recognised Morocco's independence on 2 March 1956, and Spain gave up most of its northern protectorate a few weeks later.

history.q: Which European country established a protectorate over most of Morocco with the Treaty of Fez in 1912?
history.fact: Spain received a separate zone in the north, and the French moved the seat of government from Fez to Rabat.

history.q: In January 1943, which two Allied leaders met at the Casablanca Conference?
history.fact: Meeting in the Anfa suburb of Casablanca, they announced that the Allies would accept nothing less than the Axis powers' unconditional surrender.

history.q: In 1777 Morocco is often cited as the first country to recognise the independence of which new nation?
history.fact: The 1786 Moroccan-American Treaty of Friendship is the United States' oldest unbroken treaty, and Tangier hosted its first overseas diplomatic property.

history.q: The well-preserved ruins of Volubilis, near Meknes, are mainly the remains of a city of which ancient empire?
history.fact: Volubilis grew rich exporting olive oil, and many of its floor mosaics still lie in place where they were laid.

history.q: Which great medieval traveller was born in Tangier in 1304?
history.fact: Over about 30 years Ibn Battuta covered some 117,000 km across Africa, Asia and Europe, then dictated his travels, the Rihla, back in Morocco.

history.q: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from North Africa into Iberia in 711. Which landmark still bears his name?
history.fact: Gibraltar comes from the Arabic Jabal Tariq, meaning 'Tariq's mountain'.

history.q: The English name 'Morocco' comes from which Moroccan city?
history.fact: In Arabic the country is al-Maghrib, 'the place where the sun sets', while Persian speakers still call it Marakesh.

history.q: Allied troops landed near Casablanca in November 1942 as part of which operation?
history.fact: Torch also landed troops at Oran and Algiers, and was the first major American offensive against the Axis in the European-North African theatre.

history.q: Which dynasty has reigned in Morocco since the 17th century?
history.fact: The Alaouites came to power in the 1660s, and their dynasty has reigned without interruption ever since.

history.q: Idris I founded which dynasty in 788, whose rulers went on to establish the city of Fez?
history.fact: Fez grew from twin settlements on either bank of its river; today its medina is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a maze of thousands of alleys.

history.q: Which Berber dynasty founded Marrakesh around 1070?
history.fact: Under Yusuf ibn Tashfin, the Almoravids ruled an empire that stretched from the Senegal River into Spain.

history.q: Sultan Mohammed V returned from exile in which year, paving the way to independence?
history.fact: French authorities had exiled him in 1953; Morocco's Independence Day on 18 November recalls the speech he gave after his return.

history.q: Which city was run as an international zone by several foreign powers from the 1920s until 1956?
history.fact: Interzone Tangier drew spies, bankers and writers, from Paul Bowles to William S. Burroughs, who wrote much of 'Naked Lunch' there.

history.q: Which city served as the capital of Spain's protectorate zone in northern Morocco?
history.fact: Tetouan's whitewashed medina, rebuilt by refugees from Andalusia in the late 15th century, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.q: Which Rif leader defeated a Spanish army at the Battle of Annual in 1921?
history.fact: Abd el-Krim proclaimed a Republic of the Rif, which held out until a joint French-Spanish campaign forced his surrender in 1926.

history.q: Which European king was killed at the Battle of Ksar el-Kebir, the 'Battle of the Three Kings', in 1578?
history.fact: Sebastian died without an heir, which led to Portugal's union with Spain in 1580, while the victory brought great prestige to Morocco's Ahmad al-Mansur.

history.q: Who founded the al-Qarawiyyin mosque and centre of learning in Fez in 859?
history.fact: Al-Qarawiyyin is often described as the world's oldest continuously operating educational institution.

history.q: In 1591 an army sent by Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur crossed the Sahara and defeated which empire at Tondibi?
history.fact: The army, led by the Spanish-born commander Judar Pasha, carried firearms across the desert and went on to occupy Timbuktu and Gao.

history.q: Which Alaouite sultan, reigning for 55 years from 1672, made Meknes his imperial capital?
history.fact: He ringed Meknes with tens of kilometres of walls and monumental gates; the historic city is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.q: Whose landing at Tangier in 1905 triggered the First Moroccan Crisis?
history.fact: The crisis was settled at the Algeciras Conference of 1906, which confirmed French and Spanish influence in Morocco.

history.q: The arrival of which German gunboat at Agadir in 1911 sparked the Agadir Crisis?
history.fact: Germany eventually accepted a French protectorate over Morocco in return for a slice of French territory in Central Africa.

history.q: Juba II, the Roman client king of Mauretania, married the daughter of which famous queen?
history.fact: His wife, Cleopatra Selene, was the daughter of Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony; Juba himself was a scholar who wrote books in Greek.

history.q: Which Granada-born scholar, raised in Fez, wrote the 'Description of Africa' published in 1550?
history.fact: Born al-Hasan al-Wazzan, he was captured by corsairs and presented to Pope Leo X, whose name he took.

history.q: Which Atlantic city was the Portuguese fortress of Mazagan until 1769?
history.fact: Its vaulted Portuguese Cistern, lit by a single round opening in the roof, appears in Orson Welles's film 'Othello'.

technology.q: The vast Noor complex near Ouarzazate generates electricity from what?
technology.fact: Noor, Arabic for 'light', is among the world's largest concentrated solar power complexes, using mirrors to focus desert sunshine.

technology.q: Morocco holds the world's largest reserves of which mineral resource, a key ingredient of fertilisers?
technology.fact: Phosphorus is one of the three main crop nutrients, alongside nitrogen and potassium, so Moroccan rock helps feed farms around the world.

technology.q: In 2018 Morocco opened Africa's first high-speed railway, linking Tangier with which city?
technology.fact: The Al Boraq service, named after a winged steed of Islamic tradition, cut the Tangier-Casablanca journey from nearly five hours to about two.

technology.q: Since 1997, undersea power cables have linked Morocco's electricity grid with which country?
technology.fact: The cables beneath the Strait of Gibraltar are the only electricity link between Africa and Europe.

technology.q: Which oil is pressed from the kernels of a tree that grows wild almost only in southwestern Morocco?
technology.fact: Much of it is produced by women's cooperatives, and the argan forest region is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

technology.q: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, dated in 2017 to about 300,000 years old, are among the oldest known remains of which species?
technology.fact: The find pushed back our species' known origins by about 100,000 years and suggested Homo sapiens emerged across Africa, not in a single cradle.

technology.q: The Tissint meteorite, seen falling over southern Morocco in 2011, came from which world?
technology.fact: Witnessed falls of Martian meteorites are extremely rare, and Tissint's fresh fragments preserved traces of the Red Planet's chemistry.

technology.q: What has been processed for centuries in the dye pits of Fez's Chouara Tannery?
technology.fact: Hides are softened in vats of lime and pigeon droppings, then coloured with natural dyes such as poppy, indigo and henna.

technology.q: Greenhouses on the Souss plain near Agadir make Morocco one of Europe's main suppliers of which crop?
technology.fact: Mild winters in the Souss-Massa region let growers harvest from autumn to spring, when fields in northern Europe are cold.

technology.q: Which French carmaker opened a large factory near Tangier in 2012?
technology.fact: Linked by rail to the Tanger Med port, the plant exports most of the cars it builds, many of them Dacias.

technology.q: Morocco's state phosphate company, founded in 1920, is known by which initials?
technology.fact: Founded as the Office Chérifien des Phosphates, OCP is today one of the world's largest producers of phosphate and fertilisers.

technology.q: Which town in central Morocco grew up around the country's first big phosphate mine, opened in the 1920s?
technology.fact: Khouribga sits on one of the world's richest phosphate basins; a slurry pipeline now carries the ore to the coast at Jorf Lasfar.

technology.q: Which Córdoba-born philosopher and physician served the Almohad court and died in Marrakesh in 1198?
technology.fact: His commentaries on Aristotle were so influential in medieval Europe that he was known simply as 'the Commentator'.

technology.q: Moroccan-born scientist Rachid Yazami shared the 2014 Draper Prize for pioneering work on which technology?
technology.fact: In 1980 he showed that lithium could be reversibly stored in graphite, the basis of the anode in most lithium-ion batteries.

technology.q: What part of Casablanca's Hassan II Mosque can slide open to the sky?
technology.fact: Completed in 1993, the mosque stands partly over the Atlantic, and its prayer hall can hold around 25,000 worshippers.

technology.q: What are the khettaras of Morocco's Tafilalet region?
technology.fact: Like Persian qanats, these gently sloping tunnels carry groundwater by gravity to oasis fields, marked on the surface by lines of shafts.

technology.q: What top speed do Morocco's Al Boraq high-speed trains reach in regular service?
technology.fact: During a test run in 2017, one of the trains reached 357 km/h, a rail speed record for Africa.

technology.q: What type of bridge is the Mohammed VI Bridge, opened in 2016 across the Bou Regreg valley near Rabat?
technology.fact: Its two arch-shaped pylons echo traditional city gates, and it was billed as Africa's longest cable-stayed bridge when it opened.

technology.q: Which mathematician from Marrakesh (1256-1321) wrote the influential arithmetic manual 'Talkhis a'mal al-hisab'?
technology.fact: His concise summary of arithmetic was studied, copied and commented on across North Africa for centuries.

technology.q: Fez's Dar al-Magana, built in 1357 facing the Bou Inania Madrasa, housed what device?
technology.fact: A row of windows and brass bowls once marked the hours, but exactly how its long-lost mechanism worked is still debated.

technology.q: Morocco's Earth-observation satellite Mohammed VI-A was launched in 2017 from which spaceport?
technology.fact: It rode a European Vega rocket, and a twin satellite, Mohammed VI-B, followed from the same spaceport in 2018.

technology.q: Which southern coastal town hosts a 301 MW wind farm, opened in 2014 and among Africa's largest?
technology.fact: Its 131 turbines catch the steady trade winds blowing off the Atlantic near Cape Juby.

technology.q: Perforated shell beads at least 142,000 years old, reported in 2021, were found in which cave near Essaouira?
technology.fact: They are among the oldest known personal ornaments, hinting that early humans used jewellery to signal identity.

technology.q: A 2020 study of a Spinosaurus skeleton from Morocco's Kem Kem beds revealed what swimming adaptation?
technology.fact: The tall, flexible tail was strong evidence that this giant predator propelled itself through water like a crocodile.

technology.q: Which material stores heat at the Noor Ouarzazate solar plants so they can keep generating after sunset?
technology.fact: Sun-heated salt is kept in huge insulated tanks and later used to make steam, letting the plants supply power for hours after dark.

art.q: What is zellij, a hallmark of Moroccan palaces and fountains?
art.fact: Craftsmen chip each tiny piece by hand from glazed terracotta, then fit them together into intricate geometric stars.

art.q: Which fashion designer bought and restored Marrakesh's Jardin Majorelle with Pierre Bergé in 1980?
art.fact: The garden was created by painter Jacques Majorelle, whose vivid cobalt shade is now known as 'Majorelle blue'.

art.q: Where was the 1942 film 'Casablanca' almost entirely shot?
art.fact: Apart from scenes at a Los Angeles-area airport, it was made on Warner Bros. sound stages, and it went on to win the Oscar for Best Picture.

art.q: The mud-brick ksar of Aït Benhaddou has served as a location for which film?
art.fact: The UNESCO-listed fortified village has also appeared in 'Lawrence of Arabia' and 'Game of Thrones'.

art.q: Essaouira's big annual festival celebrates which spiritual music with sub-Saharan roots?
art.fact: Gnawa musicians play iron castanets called qraqeb, building hypnotic rhythms that can carry a ceremony through the night.

art.q: Which 12th-century minaret, about 77 m tall, dominates the skyline of Marrakesh?
art.fact: Its name comes from the booksellers, the kutubiyyin, who once traded at its foot.

art.q: Roughly how tall is the minaret of Casablanca's Hassan II Mosque, completed in 1993?
art.fact: At night a laser beam shines from its summit in the direction of Mecca.

art.q: What are babouches, sold by the thousand in Moroccan souks?
art.fact: Soft, heelless and easy to slip off at the door, classic men's babouches come in a bright saffron yellow.

art.q: Which American writer, who settled in Tangier, wrote the 1949 novel 'The Sheltering Sky'?
art.fact: Bowles lived in Tangier for more than 50 years and also made landmark field recordings of traditional Moroccan music.

art.q: Which French Romantic painter filled sketchbooks during a diplomatic mission to Morocco in 1832?
art.fact: Delacroix drew on these sketches for decades, in works such as 'Jewish Wedding in Morocco'.

art.q: Which painter created 'Window at Tangier' during stays in Morocco in 1912-13?
art.fact: Matisse's room at Tangier's Grand Hotel Villa de France, the view from which he painted, is preserved for visiting art lovers.

art.q: Fez's Bou Inania and Al-Attarine madrasas, masterpieces of carved cedar and stucco, were built by which dynasty?
art.fact: Built in the 14th century, the Bou Inania is one of the few religious buildings in Morocco that non-Muslim visitors may enter.

art.q: Seville's Giralda tower began as a minaret built by which dynasty, which also raised Marrakesh's Koutoubia?
art.fact: The Giralda, the Koutoubia and Rabat's unfinished Hassan Tower are often called three sister towers.

art.q: Which Tangier author wrote the autobiographical novel 'For Bread Alone'?
art.fact: Paul Bowles's English translation appeared in 1973, almost a decade before the Arabic original was published.

art.q: Which Moroccan author won France's Prix Goncourt in 1987 for 'The Sacred Night'?
art.fact: 'The Sacred Night' continued the story begun in his earlier novel 'The Sand Child'.

art.q: Which 1956 Alfred Hitchcock thriller opens in Marrakesh?
choices: The Man Who Knew Too Much
art.fact: Starring James Stewart and Doris Day, it introduced the song 'Que Sera, Sera', which won the Oscar for Best Original Song.

art.q: Which Atlantic port is renowned as Morocco's capital of pottery?
art.fact: Safi's potters work in a hillside quarter called the Colline des Potiers, firing glazed ceramics in traditional kilns.

art.q: Which Saadian sultan built Marrakesh's El Badi Palace after the victory of 1578?
art.fact: Its name means 'the incomparable'; a century later Moulay Ismail stripped its marble and gold to adorn Meknes.

art.q: Which 1960s modernist art movement grew around Farid Belkahia, Mohamed Melehi and Mohamed Chabâa?
art.fact: Teaching at the city's fine-arts school, they drew on Amazigh motifs, crafts and calligraphy rather than European academic painting.

art.q: Orson Welles shot much of 'Othello', which won the top prize at Cannes in 1952, in which walled port?
art.fact: Essaouira, then known as Mogador, later named a seafront square after the director.

art.q: Rolling Stones guitarist Brian Jones recorded which group of musicians in a Rif village in 1968?
art.fact: The album came out in 1971 after Jones's death, and the musicians later played on the Rolling Stones' 'Continental Drift' (1989).

art.q: Which three-stringed bass lute is the central instrument of Gnawa music?
art.fact: Also called the sintir or hajhouj, it has a skin-covered body and is played by the maâlem, the master musician who leads the ceremony.

art.q: Which 1970s Casablanca group, often dubbed 'the Rolling Stones of Africa', transformed Moroccan popular music?
art.fact: Formed in Casablanca's Hay Mohammadi district, the band blended Gnawa rhythms, Sufi chants and sung poetry about everyday life.

art.q: Which director made 'Ali Zaoua' (2000), about street children in Casablanca?
art.fact: Ayouch cast children who really lived on Casablanca's streets, and the film became one of Morocco's best-known abroad.

art.q: Essaouira's woodworkers are famous for marquetry made from the burl of which fragrant local tree?
art.fact: The thuya's knotted root burl is polished to a rich swirling grain and often inlaid with lemonwood or mother-of-pearl.

politics.q: How does Morocco's constitution define the country's system of government?
politics.fact: The 2011 constitution describes Morocco as a constitutional, democratic, parliamentary and social monarchy.

politics.q: What is the capital of Morocco?
politics.fact: Rabat has been the seat of government since 1912, and its blend of historic and modern districts is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

politics.q: Which king acceded to the Moroccan throne in July 1999?
politics.fact: Mohammed VI succeeded his father, Hassan II, who had reigned for 38 years.

politics.q: Which king reigned in Morocco from 1961 until 1999?
politics.fact: He commissioned Casablanca's vast Hassan II Mosque, completed in 1993.

politics.q: Which continental organisation did Morocco rejoin in January 2017?
politics.fact: Morocco had been outside the organisation since 1984, when it left the AU's predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity.

politics.q: What emblem appears in the centre of Morocco's red flag?
politics.fact: The green interlaced pentagram, added in 1915, is known as the Seal of Solomon.

politics.q: In which year did Moroccans approve, by referendum, a new constitution that expanded the powers of parliament and the head of government?
politics.fact: Approved on 1 July 2011, the constitution also made Tamazight an official language alongside Arabic.

politics.q: How many chambers does Morocco's parliament have?
politics.fact: The directly elected House of Representatives sits alongside the House of Councillors, chosen by local councils and professional bodies.

politics.q: Morocco's national motto is 'God, the Homeland, ...' what?
politics.fact: In Arabic it reads 'Allah, al-Watan, al-Malik', and it is written into the constitution.

politics.q: Which language became an official language alongside Arabic in Morocco's 2011 constitution?
politics.fact: Millions of Moroccans speak Amazigh languages, chiefly Tarifit in the north, Central Atlas Tamazight and Tashelhit in the south.

politics.q: Which party led Moroccan governments from 2011 to 2021?
choices: The Socialist Union of Popular Forces
politics.fact: Its leaders Abdelilah Benkirane and then Saadeddine Othmani served in turn as head of government.

politics.q: Morocco's 2004 reform of the Moudawana overhauled which area of law?
politics.fact: The reform raised the minimum marriage age to 18 and gave women more rights in divorce and child custody.

politics.q: In 1957 Sultan Mohammed V adopted which new title?
politics.fact: The change, a year after independence, marked Morocco's transformation into a modern kingdom.

politics.q: On which date does Morocco celebrate Throne Day under Mohammed VI?
politics.fact: Throne Day marks the king's accession, while 18 November is celebrated as Independence Day.

politics.q: Under the 2011 constitution, the king appoints the head of government from which party?
choices: The party with the most members nationwide
The party that wins the most seats in the House of Representatives
The party that wins the most seats in the House of Councillors
politics.fact: The rule, in Article 47, ties the choice of head of government directly to the result of the parliamentary elections.

politics.q: In which year did Morocco join the United Nations?
politics.fact: Morocco became a UN member on 12 November 1956, just months after independence.

politics.q: Morocco's constitution gives the king which religious title?
politics.fact: As Amir al-Mu'minin, the king is charged with ensuring respect for Islam and guaranteeing the free exercise of beliefs.

politics.q: Nationalist leader Allal al-Fassi was a founding figure of which party?
politics.fact: Istiqlal means 'independence' in Arabic, and the party was at the heart of the movement to end the protectorate.

politics.q: In which year did Morocco adopt its first constitution by referendum?
politics.fact: The 1962 text, approved under Hassan II, has since been revised or replaced several times, most recently in 2011.

politics.q: In 1987 Morocco applied to join which organisation, which turned the bid down because Morocco is not a European state?
politics.fact: Ties deepened anyway, and in 2008 the European Union granted Morocco 'advanced status' in its relations with the bloc.

politics.q: In 2004 the United States designated Morocco as what?
choices: A member of the Five Eyes
politics.fact: The same year, the two countries signed a free-trade agreement, which came into force in 2006.

politics.q: Which veteran socialist led Morocco's 'government of alternance' formed in 1998?
politics.fact: A long-time opposition figure who had lived in exile, he was appointed by Hassan II in a landmark opening to the opposition.

politics.q: How many seats does Morocco's House of Representatives have?
politics.fact: Members serve five-year terms and are elected from local constituencies and regional lists.

politics.q: The Marrakesh Agreement, signed in April 1994, established which international body?
politics.fact: Signed by ministers from more than 120 countries, it concluded the Uruguay Round of global trade talks.

politics.q: In which year did nationalists issue Morocco's Manifesto of Independence, remembered with a holiday every 11 January?
politics.fact: Presented by the Istiqlal Party, the manifesto called for full independence under Sultan Mohammed V.

current-affairs.q: At the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, Morocco became the first African team to reach which stage?
current-affairs.fact: Morocco lost 2-0 to France in the semi-final and finished fourth after a third-place play-off against Croatia.

current-affairs.q: In December 2024, FIFA confirmed Morocco would co-host the 2030 World Cup with which two countries?
current-affairs.fact: Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay will also each stage one opening match to mark the tournament's centenary.

current-affairs.q: In September 2023, a deadly earthquake struck villages in which mountain range south-west of Marrakesh?
current-affairs.fact: The magnitude 6.8 quake killed nearly 3,000 people and badly damaged historic sites such as the 12th-century Tinmel Mosque.

current-affairs.q: Which country hosted the Africa Cup of Nations that kicked off in December 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Morocco had last hosted the continent's biggest football tournament in 1988.

current-affairs.q: Morocco knocked out which team on penalties in the round of 16 at the 2022 World Cup?
current-affairs.fact: Spanish-born defender Achraf Hakimi sealed the shoot-out with a cheeky chipped 'Panenka' penalty.

current-affairs.q: Moroccan defender Achraf Hakimi won the UEFA Champions League in May 2025 with which club?
current-affairs.fact: He scored the opening goal as the Paris club beat Inter 5-0 in Munich to win the trophy for the first time.

current-affairs.q: At the Tokyo Olympics in August 2021, Soufiane El Bakkali won gold in which event?
current-affairs.fact: He was the first non-Kenyan to win the men's Olympic steeplechase since 1980, and he retained his title at Paris 2024.

current-affairs.q: In July 2024, King Mohammed VI marked how many years on the throne?
current-affairs.fact: He acceded on 23 July 1999, succeeding his father, Hassan II.

current-affairs.q: Which medal did Morocco's men's football team win at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: They thrashed Egypt 6-0 in the bronze-medal match, earning Morocco's first Olympic medal in football.

current-affairs.q: Who was appointed Morocco's head of government after the September 2021 elections?
current-affairs.fact: His National Rally of Independents (RNI) won the most seats, ending a decade of PJD-led governments.

current-affairs.q: Which coach led Morocco to the 2022 World Cup semi-finals only months after taking charge?
current-affairs.fact: Appointed in August 2022, the former Morocco defender had just won the CAF Champions League with Wydad Casablanca.

current-affairs.q: Whose header beat Portugal 1-0 in the 2022 World Cup quarter-final?
current-affairs.fact: The goal knocked out a Portugal side featuring Cristiano Ronaldo and sparked celebrations from Casablanca to Paris.

current-affairs.q: Which Moroccan city hosted the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in October 2023?
current-affairs.fact: It was the first time in 50 years that the meetings were held in Africa, and they went ahead weeks after the Al Haouz earthquake.

current-affairs.q: Morocco made its Women's World Cup debut in 2023. Which team beat them 6-0 in their opening match?
current-affairs.fact: Morocco bounced back to beat South Korea and Colombia and reach the round of 16 at their first attempt.

current-affairs.q: Which country beat hosts Morocco 2-1 in the Women's Africa Cup of Nations final in July 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Despite the defeat, Morocco's run to the final earned the team its first-ever place at a Women's World Cup.

current-affairs.q: Which Real Madrid attacker chose in 2024 to represent Morocco rather than Spain?
current-affairs.fact: Born in Málaga to a Moroccan father, he had played one friendly for Spain in 2021 before switching allegiance.

current-affairs.q: Roughly how many tourist arrivals did Morocco record in 2024, a national record?
current-affairs.fact: Arrivals rose by about a fifth on 2023, helped by new air routes and Moroccans living abroad coming home to visit.

current-affairs.q: Morocco topped its 2022 World Cup group after beating which European team 2-0?
current-affairs.fact: Unbeaten in the group, Morocco finished ahead of Croatia, Belgium and Canada.

current-affairs.q: Which club won the 2022 FIFA Club World Cup, played in Morocco in February 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Real Madrid beat Saudi side Al-Hilal 5-3 in the final in Rabat.

current-affairs.q: Moroccan director Asmae El Moudir won the Un Certain Regard directing prize at Cannes in 2023 for which documentary?
current-affairs.fact: She rebuilt her Casablanca childhood neighbourhood in miniature, with clay figurines, to tease out her family's memories.

current-affairs.q: In 2022 Yassine Bounou won which Spanish award for La Liga's best goalkeeping record with Sevilla?
current-affairs.fact: The trophy goes to the La Liga goalkeeper with the lowest ratio of goals conceded per game over the season.

current-affairs.q: Which Moroccan city did UNESCO name World Book Capital for 2026?
current-affairs.fact: The year-long title recognises a city's programme to promote books, reading and publishing.

current-affairs.q: Which Moroccan tradition did UNESCO add to its intangible cultural heritage list in December 2021?
current-affairs.fact: In tbourida, rows of horsemen in traditional dress charge in unison and fire their muskets at the same instant.

current-affairs.q: Which Casablanca club won the CAF Champions League in May 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Wydad beat Egypt's Al Ahly 2-0 in a one-off final at the Mohammed V Stadium in Casablanca.

current-affairs.q: In 2020 UNESCO recognised couscous traditions after a joint bid by Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and which other country?
current-affairs.fact: The shared nomination celebrated the knowledge, know-how and practices around couscous across the Maghreb.

society.q: Morocco's 2024 census put the population at roughly how many?
society.fact: The HCP counted 36.8 million, up 3 million since 2014, with annual growth slowing to 0.85%; more than 60% of Moroccans now live in urban areas.

society.q: In February 2023, Morocco's annual inflation rate briefly rose above what level, driven mainly by food prices?
society.fact: Inflation hit 10.1% in February 2023, the highest in decades; the 2022 average had been 6.6%, and it fell back below 1% during 2024.

society.q: In February 2025, King Mohammed VI asked Moroccans to forgo which Eid al-Adha tradition because drought had shrunk the national herd?
society.fact: Livestock numbers had fallen by about 38% since 2016 after years of drought; King Hassan II made a similar appeal in 1966.

society.q: By the early 2020s, which industry had overtaken phosphates as Morocco's top export sector?
society.fact: Renault in Tangier and Stellantis in Kenitra made Morocco Africa's largest car producer, with vehicle exports topping 100 billion dirhams a year by 2022.

society.q: Morocco's unemployment rate, as measured by the HCP, stood at roughly what in 2024?
society.fact: The 13.3% rate meant about 1.6 million people were jobless; among 15 to 24-year-olds it was about 37%, and urban unemployment far exceeded rural.

society.q: In December 2023, Morocco launched a programme of monthly payments to low-income families with children, known as what?
society.fact: Eligible households, enrolled through the Unified Social Register, receive at least 500 dirhams a month; the scheme replaced several older subsidies.

society.q: In late September 2025, youth protests under the banner 'GenZ 212' spread across Moroccan cities calling mainly for better what?
society.fact: Organised on the Discord app, protesters contrasted spending on 2030 World Cup stadiums with the state of public hospitals and schools.

society.q: In 2021, Morocco's parliament passed a law legalising the cultivation of which crop for medical and industrial use?
society.fact: A national agency, ANRAC, issues licences in the Rif provinces of Al Hoceima, Chefchaouen and Taounate, where the first legal harvest came in 2023.

society.q: In April 2025, King Mohammed VI launched works to extend the Al Boraq high-speed rail line from Kenitra to which city?
society.fact: The 430 km extension via Rabat and Casablanca is due to open before the 2030 World Cup, cutting Tangier-Marrakesh journeys to under three hours.

society.q: In May 2024, Morocco began phasing out its butane gas subsidy by raising the price of a 12 kg bottle from 40 dirhams to what?
society.fact: The price had been frozen since 1990; a further rise to 60 dirhams followed in 2025, with the savings earmarked for direct social aid.

society.q: Launched in January 2024, Morocco's 'Daam Sakane' programme offers first-time buyers of a new home what?
choices: Exemption from VAT on the purchase
A direct grant of up to 100,000 dirhams
society.fact: Buyers get 100,000 dirhams for homes under 300,000 dirhams and 70,000 for those up to 700,000; Moroccans living abroad are also eligible.

society.q: In December 2022, Morocco replaced the RAMED scheme for poor households with what?
society.fact: The switch moved around 4 million households into the main CNSS-run compulsory health insurance system as part of the generalisation of social protection.

society.q: In 2022, a large seawater desalination plant began supplying drinking water and irrigation to which Moroccan city and its farming hinterland?
society.fact: The Chtouka plant, among Africa's largest, supplies the Souss region's tomato and citrus farms; a far bigger plant for Casablanca followed.

society.q: Casablanca opened two new tram lines, T3 and T4, in which year?
society.fact: The lines added 25 km and 39 stations in September 2024, months after the city's first bus rapid transit routes opened.

society.q: In 2022, Morocco paid direct subsidies to which group to offset soaring diesel prices, fuel subsidies having been abolished in 2015?
society.fact: Lorry, bus and taxi operators received payments in several rounds during 2022 and 2023 to head off strikes over fuel costs.

society.q: Remittances from Moroccans living abroad reached a record of roughly how much in 2023?
society.fact: Transfers of about 115 billion dirhams exceeded foreign direct investment and made the diaspora, roughly 5 million strong, a pillar of the economy.

society.q: In December 2024, Morocco announced proposed reforms to which legal code, including on marriage age and child custody?
society.fact: The proposals followed a review ordered by the king in 2022 and came two decades after the landmark 2004 reform.

society.q: To curb inflation, Bank Al-Maghrib raised its key policy rate in three steps between September 2022 and March 2023 to what?
society.fact: It was the first tightening since 2008; the bank began cutting again in June 2024 as inflation fell below 2%.

society.q: Morocco's 2024 census measured a fertility rate of roughly how many children per woman?
society.fact: At 1.97 the rate fell below replacement level for the first time; the HCP expects the population to peak at about 40 million before declining.

society.q: In April 2023, the IMF approved a two-year precautionary Flexible Credit Line for Morocco worth about how much?
society.fact: The FCL is reserved for countries with very strong policy records; Morocco said it would treat the line as insurance rather than draw on it.

society.q: The 'Awrach' programme launched in 2022 aimed to create how many temporary jobs over two years?
society.fact: Participants on public worksites were paid at least the minimum wage with social cover; about 100,000 people were placed in the first year.

society.q: In December 2023, Morocco's government ended a wave of teachers' strikes by agreeing a pay rise of how much a month?
society.fact: The rise was paid in two 750-dirham instalments in 2024 and 2025 and was coupled with a new unified statute for education staff.

society.q: A social agreement signed in April 2022 raised Morocco's private-sector minimum wage (SMIG) by what in total over two years?
society.fact: The rise came in two 5% steps in September 2022 and 2023; a further 10% over two years was agreed in April 2024.

society.q: The 'Intelaka' programme, launched in February 2020, offered Moroccans what?
society.fact: Banks offered loans at about 2% interest, backed by state guarantees, to young people and small firms, with a 1.75% rate in rural areas.

society.q: Morocco's 2023 finance law set corporate tax rates to converge gradually by 2026 on a standard rate of what?
society.fact: Large firms with profits above 100 million dirhams converge on 35%, and banks and insurers on 40%, under the same four-year schedule.

general.q: Which narrow strait separates Morocco from Spain?
general.fact: At its narrowest the strait is only about 14 km wide, and on clear days Spain is visible from the Moroccan shore.

general.q: What is the currency of Morocco?
general.fact: The name dirham, shared with the UAE's currency, ultimately comes from the ancient Greek drachma.

general.q: Which slow-cooked Moroccan stew takes its name from the conical clay pot it is cooked in?
general.fact: The cone traps rising steam, which condenses and drips back down, keeping the meat and vegetables moist.

general.q: Which town in the Rif Mountains is famous for its blue-washed streets?
general.fact: Founded in 1471 as a small fortress, Chefchaouen is often called Morocco's 'Blue Pearl'.

general.q: Which mountain range stretches across Morocco, separating the Atlantic coast from the Sahara?
general.fact: Greek myth told that the Titan Atlas, who held up the sky, was turned to stone here and became these mountains.

general.q: Which Marrakesh square comes alive each evening with storytellers, musicians and food stalls?
general.fact: In 2001 its living traditions were among the first proclaimed Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO.

general.q: What is Morocco's traditional drink of hospitality?
general.fact: Hosts pour the sweet tea from a height to raise a light froth in each small glass.

general.q: What is Morocco's largest city?
general.fact: Its name means 'white house' in Spanish; locals often call it 'Casa' or by its Arabic name, Dar el Beida.

general.q: Which brimless felt hat takes its name from a Moroccan city?
general.fact: Also known as the tarboosh, the red fez became fashionable across the Ottoman Empire in the 19th century.

general.q: Which peak, at 4,167 m, is the highest in North Africa?
general.fact: Toubkal is usually climbed over two days from the village of Imlil, in the High Atlas south of Marrakesh.

general.q: Which Moroccan runner set the men's 1,500 m world record of 3:26.00 in 1998?
general.fact: He won Olympic gold in both the 1,500 m and 5,000 m at Athens 2004, and his 1,500 m and mile records stood for decades.

general.q: In 1984 Nawal El Moutawakel became Morocco's first Olympic champion in which event?
general.fact: Her win in Los Angeles made her the first woman from an Arab or Muslim-majority country to take Olympic gold.

general.q: What is the everyday spoken Arabic of Morocco called?
general.fact: Darija mixes Arabic with Amazigh, French and Spanish words; a car, for example, is often a 'tomobil'.

general.q: Which monkey lives wild in the cedar forests of Morocco's Middle Atlas?
general.fact: It is Africa's only macaque, and a small colony also famously lives on the Rock of Gibraltar.

general.q: Which festive Moroccan pie combines savoury pigeon or chicken with a dusting of sugar and cinnamon?
general.fact: Its paper-thin warqa pastry is made by dabbing dough onto a hot pan, one delicate sheet at a time.

general.q: Which sea of dunes rises beside the desert village of Merzouga?
general.fact: Some of its wind-sculpted dunes rise around 150 m above the surrounding stony desert.

general.q: Which animals are famously seen perched in argan trees in southwestern Morocco?
general.fact: Goats clamber up the thorny branches to nibble the fruit, a sight that has become a roadside attraction.

general.q: Which script is used to write Tamazight on many Moroccan public signs?
general.fact: A standard form, Neo-Tifinagh, was adopted for Morocco by the Royal Institute of Amazigh Culture in 2003.

general.q: Which Middle Atlas town, nicknamed 'the Switzerland of Morocco', holds Africa's record low temperature of -23.9 °C?
general.fact: Built by the French in the 1920s, its alpine-style chalets and red roofs surround a famous stone lion statue.

general.q: The town of Taliouine, between Ouarzazate and Taroudant, is famous for which costly spice?
general.fact: Each autumn the crocus flowers are picked by hand at dawn and their red stigmas dried; a kilogram needs some 150,000 flowers.

general.q: Kelaat M'Gouna, in the Dades valley, holds a festival every May celebrating which flower harvest?
general.fact: Damask roses grown in hedges between the fields are distilled into rosewater and oils.

general.q: The prized Medjool date variety originated in which Moroccan oasis region?
general.fact: In 1927 a handful of offshoots were sent to the United States, saving the variety from a palm disease and seeding orchards there.

general.q: Roughly how far do runners travel in the multi-stage Marathon des Sables across the Moroccan Sahara?
general.fact: Since 1986, competitors have carried their own food and kit across dunes, stony plains and dry riverbeds over about six stages.

general.q: Into which body of water does the Moulouya, one of Morocco's longest rivers, flow?
general.fact: Its mouth near Saïdia is a protected wetland that draws flamingos and migrating birds.

general.q: The Caves of Hercules, whose sea opening is said to resemble a map of Africa, lie near which cape west of Tangier?
general.fact: Legend says Hercules rested in the cave before one of his twelve labours.
